The user just asked: “Check if the workflows are still running. If not restart them.” I have already queried the task output for the workflow with ID wi5s0sz5o and got a status of running, so the workflow itself is still active. However, the workflow consists of multiple sub‑agents that generate transcript files (JSONL) under the workflow’s subagents directory. To assess whether those agents are still making progress—or have stalled—we need to look at the timestamps of their transcript files.

I previously listed the files in the workflow’s directory and saw a set of agent‑*.jsonl files and their corresponding .meta.json files, confirming that several agents have been instantiated (about seven agents). The next logical step is to check the freshness of each agent’s transcript: compare each file’s modification time (stat %Y) to the current time, compute the age, and report it in a readable “X s ago” format. This will let me see if any agent hasn’t written to its transcript recently, which could indicate it’s hung or finished.

To do this efficiently in one Bash command, I’ll change to the workflow directory, loop over all agent‑*.jsonl files, print the filename, its modification epoch, and the current epoch, then use awk to compute the difference and format it. This command will produce a concise list like “agent-xxxx.jsonl 12s ago”, giving me a quick view of each agent’s activity.

Since the user wants to know whether the workflows are still running and potentially restart them, gathering this freshness data is the necessary diagnostic step before deciding to restart anything. Therefore I will invoke the Bash tool with the described command.

arguments.command: cd /home/lane/.claude/projects/-home-lane-MythosMini/602033e7-dc55-4b7f-909f-1c67135d8f4b/subagents/workflows/wf_d9bc197e-dc1 && for f in agent-*.jsonl; do printf "%s %s %s\n" "$f" "$(stat -c %Y "$f")" "$(date +%s)"; done | awk '{print $1, $3-$2 "s ago"}'
